---
title: "9. Show what the model predicts"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

## Plots of Model Predictions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- Perhaps the most versatile and useful tool of the applied data analyst is the ability to plot model predictions
  - The most effective way to understand a model is almost always to examine what the model predicts!
    - Predictions are especially important when the model is nonlinear
      - E.g., Because of a quadratic/polynomial term for an IV, because the DV is categorical, etc.
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/mize-kincaid-2025.png){fig-alt="Published figure: predicted psychological well-being ratings by age, a curve that dips in midlife and rises at older ages."}

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
From [Mize and Kincaid (2025)](/research/mize_kincaid_asr_2025.qmd)
:::
:::
::::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss.dta", clear
drop if year < 2000
drop if employed != 1

// Linear regression model with age and age-squared
qui regress wages c.age##c.age i.woman i.college i.race
qui margins, at(age=(18(2)90))

// 9.a - Plot predictions for age
marginsplot, plotopts(msym(none)) xlab(20(10)90) ylab(0(5)30) ///
    recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ///
    ytitle("Hourly Wages") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[9.a] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age of Worker")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_a-preds.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_a-preds.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.a] Predicted hourly wages by age from 18 to 90 with a dashed 95% confidence interval: wages rise from about 8 dollars at 18 to a peak of about 20 dollars in the mid-50s and then fall to about 11 dollars at 90."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.a] Predicted hourly wages by age from 18 to 90 with a 95% confidence interval: wages rise to a peak in the mid-50s and then fall."
library(foreign)            # load Stata datasets
library(ggplot2)            # main graphics package
library(dplyr)              # data manipulation tools
library(marginaleffects)    # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)         # Mize's graphics scheme

## Use cleanplots colors, markers, lines, and theme for all graphs ##
cleanplots_defaults()
theme_update(plot.title.position = "plot")   # titles start at left edge of graph

# General Social Survey Data
gss <- droplevels(read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss.dta"))
gss_emp <- droplevels(filter(gss, year >= 2000, employed == 1))

# Linear regression model with age and age-squared
wage_mod <- lm(wages ~ poly(age, 2, raw = TRUE) + woman + college + race, data = gss_emp)

# 9.a - Plot predictions for age
plot_predictions(wage_mod, condition = "age") +
  labs(x = "Age in Years", y = "Hourly Wages",
       title = "[9.a] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age of Worker") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 90, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 30))
```

:::

### Adding distributional information

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// Allow the age effect to differ for men and women
qui regress wages c.age##c.age##i.woman i.college i.race
qui margins, at(age=(18(2)90) woman=(0 1))

// 9.b - Histogram to show distribution of age
marginsplot, plotopts(msym(i)) ///
    recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ///
    ytitle("Hourly Wages") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[9.b] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age of Worker") ///
    addplot(hist age, width(1) lcol(gs10) ///
    fcol(none) yaxis(2) yscale(range(0 0.15) off alt axis(2)) ///
    legend(order(3 "Men" 4 "Women")) xlab(20(10)90) ylab(0(5)30))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_b-preds_hist.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_b-preds_hist.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.b] Predicted hourly wages by age for men and women with 95% confidence intervals, and a histogram of age along the bottom of the graph: most workers are between about 20 and 65, and few are older than 70, where the confidence intervals widen."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.b] Predicted hourly wages by age for men and women with 95% confidence intervals, and a histogram of age along the bottom of the graph: most workers are between about 20 and 65, and few are older than 70, where the confidence intervals widen."
# Allow the age effect to differ for men and women
wage_int <- lm(wages ~ poly(age, 2, raw = TRUE) * woman + college + race, data = gss_emp)

# 9.b - Add a histogram of age to the bottom of the plot
plot_predictions(wage_int, condition = c("age", "woman")) +
  geom_histogram(data = gss_emp, binwidth = 1, fill = NA, color = "gray70",
                 aes(x = age, y = after_stat(count / max(count) * 5)),
                 inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Age in Years", y = "Hourly Wages", color = "", fill = "",
       title = "[9.b] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age of Worker") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 90, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 30))
```

## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// Generate variables to make rugs on plot
gen pipe = "|" if age != .     // What rug looks like
gen agerand = age + rnormal(0,1) // "jitter" age
gen where = 0                  // Where on y-axis to put 1st rug
gen where2 = 1.2               // Where on y-axis to put 2nd rug

// 9.c - Rug plots: separate rugs for men and women (faded colors)
marginsplot, plotopts(msym(i)) ///
    recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ///
    ytitle("Hourly Wages") xtitle("Age in Years") ///
    title("[9.c] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age of Worker") ///
    addplot(scatter where2 agerand if woman == 0, ///
        ms(none) mlabel(pipe) mlabcol(red*.6) mlabpos(0) || ///
    scatter where agerand if woman == 1, ///
        ms(none) mlabel(pipe) mlabcol(eltblue*.6) mlabpos(0) ///
    legend(order(3 "Men" 4 "Women")) xlab(20(10)90) ylab(0(5)30))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_c-preds_rug.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_c-preds_rug.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.c] The same predictions with two rug plots along the bottom, a faded red rug for men and a faded blue rug for women: each tick marks a worker's (jittered) age, so the rugs are densest between about 20 and 65."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.c] The same predictions with two rug plots along the bottom, a faded red rug for men above a faded blue rug for women: each tick marks a worker's (jittered) age, so the rugs are densest between about 20 and 65."
# 9.c - Rug plot: "jitter" age so can better see where the data is; colors faded
dat_rug <- insight::get_data(wage_int)                          # estimation sample
dat_rug$age_j <- dat_rug$age + runif(nrow(dat_rug), -0.4, 0.4)  # jitter
dat_rug$rug_y <- ifelse(dat_rug$woman == "Men", 1.2, 0)         # men's rug above women's

plot_predictions(wage_int, condition = c("age", "woman")) +
  geom_point(data = dat_rug, aes(x = age_j, y = rug_y, color = woman), shape = "|",
             size = 3, alpha = 0.06, inherit.aes = FALSE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Age in Years", y = "Hourly Wages", color = "", fill = "",
       title = "[9.c] Predicted Hourly Wages Based on Age of Worker",
       subtitle = "With rug plot to show distribution of age (jittered)") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(20, 90, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, 5)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 30))
```

:::

### Plotting predictions for nominal vs continuous variables

- **For IVs treated as continuous**: sort the *x*-axis left to right by values of the IV, make predictions at most or all levels of the IV, and connect the lines between the predictions
  - This helps visually mirror the assumption of continuity in how you modeled the IV
- **For IVs treated as nominal**: *x*-axis sorting is often arbitrary\*, dots or bars should clearly represent distinct predictions being made for each grouping, and **there should be no lines connecting** the predictions
  - Lines connecting predictions suggest continuity, whereas nominal IVs have no ordering information
  - Be consistent in ordering across figures, tables, etc.
- For ordinal variables modeled as nominal, use the logical order in tables and graphs (e.g., "high school degree" left of "college degree")

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta", clear

tab samesexop
gen samesexAW = samesexop
lab var samesexAW "Same Sex Relationship Always Wrong"
recode samesexAW 1=1 2/4 = 0
lab def ssaw 0"Not Always Wrong" 1"Always Wrong"
lab val samesexAW ssaw
tab samesexop samesexAW

drop if missing(samesexAW, reltrad, woman, college, race3, faminc, age, year)

*Omitting Catholic -- Only including surveys beginning in 2000
qui logit samesexAW ib4.reltrad i.woman i.college i.race3 c.faminc c.age ///
    if year >= 2000

*Get predictions for each category
margins reltrad

// 9.d - Use recast(scatter) for a dot plot for a nominal IV
marginsplot, recast(scatter) ylab(0(.2)1) ciopts(col(*.4)) xtitle(" ") ///
    xlab(, angle(45)) ytitle("Pr(Always Wrong)") ///
    title("[9.d] Predicted Probability of Viewing Same-Sex Relationships As 'Always Wrong'", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("By Religious Affiliation")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_d-preds_nominal.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_d-preds_nominal.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.d] Dot plot of the predicted probability of viewing same-sex relationships as always wrong for seven religious traditions, with 95% confidence intervals: highest for Evangelicals (about .71), about .38 to .49 for Mainline Protestants, Black Protestants, Catholics, and Other Faith, and lowest for Jewish (.18) and Nonaffiliated (.19) respondents."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.d] Dot plot of the predicted probability of viewing same-sex relationships as always wrong for seven religious traditions, with 95% confidence intervals: highest for Evangelicals and lowest for Jewish and Nonaffiliated respondents."
# General Social Survey Data (religious tradition ex)
cda_gss <- droplevels(read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta"))

# DV: same-sex relationships are always wrong (1) vs not (0)
cda_gss$samesexAW <- as.numeric(cda_gss$samesexop == "always wrong")

gss_rel <- cda_gss %>%
  filter(year >= 2000) %>%
  filter(!is.na(samesexAW), !is.na(reltrad), !is.na(woman), !is.na(college),
         !is.na(race3), !is.na(faminc), !is.na(age)) %>%
  droplevels()

logit_rel <- glm(samesexAW ~ reltrad + woman + college + race3 + faminc + age,
                 family = binomial, data = gss_rel)

# 9.d - The default plot for a nominal IV is a dot plot (which is good)
plot_predictions(logit_rel, condition = "reltrad") +
  labs(x = "", y = "Pr(Always Wrong)",
       title = "[9.d] Predicted Probability of Viewing Same-Sex Relationships As 'Always Wrong'",
       subtitle = "By Religious Affiliation") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

:::

## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// 9.e - DON'T DO THIS! marginsplot's default connects lines for a nominal IV
marginsplot, ylab(0(.2)1) ciopts(col(*.4)) xtitle(" ") ///
    xlab(, angle(45)) ytitle("Pr(Always Wrong)") ///
    title("[9.e] {bf:Don't Do This:} Do Not Connect Lines of Predictions for Nominal IVs", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("Connected lines suggest a continuous IV which this is not")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_e-preds_nominal-BAD.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_e-preds_nominal-BAD.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.e] Don't do this: the same predicted probabilities for the seven religious traditions connected by a line, which wrongly suggests the religious traditions are ordered."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.e] Don't do this: the same predicted probabilities for the seven religious traditions connected by a line, which wrongly suggests the religious traditions are ordered."
# 9.e - DON'T DO THIS! Connected lines suggest a continuous IV, which this is not
pred_rel <- plot_predictions(logit_rel, condition = "reltrad", draw = FALSE)

ggplot(pred_rel, aes(x = reltrad, y = estimate, group = 1)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = .2) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Pr(Always Wrong)",
       title = "[9.e] Don't Do This: Do Not Connect Lines of Predictions for Nominal IVs",
       subtitle = "Connected lines suggest a continuous IV which this is not") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

## Confidence intervals and statistical significance

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
- "Fun" game: guess which of the following group differences (b~0~ vs. b~1~) are significant at the 95% level (two-tailed test)
- The dependent variable is continuous
  - The independent variable (b) is binary with two values (0 and 1)
- The test for significance can be\*:
  - A *t*-test
  - An ANOVA
  - A linear regression model
  - A Wald test for equality of predictions

\*Fun fact: these are all identical tests in this simple case...
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
![](images/spiderman-pointing.jpeg){fig-alt="Meme of several Spider-Men pointing at each other."}
:::
::::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// Simulated data: two groups (b = 0 vs b = 1) with a true difference of 5
clear
set seed 30004
set obs 1000

gen b = .
replace b = 0 in 1/500
replace b = 1 in 501/1000
gen y10 = 50 + 5*b + rnormal(0,10)
gen y20 = 50 + 5*b + rnormal(0,20)
gen y25 = 50 + 5*b + rnormal(0,25)
gen y30 = 50 + 5*b + rnormal(0,30)

* Estimate the models and save the predictions for each outcome
foreach y in y30 y20 y25 {
    qui reg `y' i.b
    qui margins, at(b=(0 1)) post
    est store pr_`y'
}

// 9.g - Error term has SD of 30
est restore pr_y30
coefplot, vertical ciop(recast(rcap) col(gs10)) ylab(45(1)60) ///
    xlab(1 "b = 0" 2 "b = 1") ytitle("y-hat") ///
    title("[9.g] Predictions and 95% Confidence Intervals - Linear Regression Model")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_g-CIs_y30.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_g-CIs_y30.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.g] Predicted y and 95% confidence intervals for b = 0 (about 49.1) and b = 1 (about 55.9): the two confidence intervals do not overlap."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.g] Predicted y and 95% confidence intervals for b = 0 and b = 1: the two confidence intervals do not overlap."
# Simulated data: two groups (b = 0 vs b = 1) with a true difference of 5
# R and Stata draw different random numbers; this seed gives the same pattern as Stata's
set.seed(43940)
sim <- data.frame(b = factor(rep(c(0, 1), each = 500)))
sim$y10 <- 50 + 5 * (sim$b == 1) + rnorm(1000, 0, 10)
sim$y20 <- 50 + 5 * (sim$b == 1) + rnorm(1000, 0, 20)
sim$y25 <- 50 + 5 * (sim$b == 1) + rnorm(1000, 0, 25)
sim$y30 <- 50 + 5 * (sim$b == 1) + rnorm(1000, 0, 30)

# Plot predictions and CIs for the two groups; optionally show the test of the difference
ci_plot <- function(y, label, show_p = FALSE) {
  m <- lm(reformulate("b", y), data = sim)
  p <- avg_comparisons(m, variables = "b")$p.value
  ggplot(avg_predictions(m, variables = "b"), aes(x = b, y = estimate)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = .1, color = "gray60") +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("b = 0", "b = 1")) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(45, 60, 1)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(45, 60)) +
    labs(x = "", y = "y-hat",
         title = paste0("[", label, "] Predictions and 95% Confidence Intervals - Linear Regression Model"),
         subtitle = if (show_p) paste0("Group Difference (b0 vs b1) is significant: ",
                                       ifelse(p < .001, "p < 0.001", paste("p =", round(p, 3))),
                                       " (two-tailed test)"))
}

# 9.g - Error term has SD of 30
ci_plot("y30", "9.g")
```

### With the significance tests

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// 9.j - Error term has SD of 30
est restore pr_y30
lincom 2._at - 1._at    // test of the difference in predictions

coefplot, vertical ciop(recast(rcap) col(gs10)) ylab(45(1)60) ///
    xlab(1 "b = 0" 2 "b = 1") ytitle("y-hat") ///
    title("[9.j] Predictions and 95% Confidence Intervals - Linear Regression Model") ///
    subtitle("Group Difference (b{sub: 0} vs b{sub: 1}) is significant: {it: p} < 0.001 (two-tailed test)")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_j-CIs_y30_p.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_j-CIs_y30_p.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.j] The SD 30 predictions again, with the subtitle: Group difference (b0 vs b1) is significant, p < 0.001 (two-tailed test)."}

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.j] The SD 30 predictions again, with the subtitle: Group difference (b0 vs b1) is significant, p < 0.001 (two-tailed test)."
# 9.j - Error term has SD of 30
avg_comparisons(lm(y30 ~ b, data = sim), variables = "b")

<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_l-CIs_y25_p.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.l] The SD 25 predictions again, whose confidence intervals overlap, with the subtitle: Group difference (b0 vs b1) is significant, p = 0.032 (two-tailed test)."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.l] The SD 25 predictions again, whose confidence intervals overlap, with the subtitle saying the group difference is significant."
# 9.l - Error term has SD of 25
avg_comparisons(lm(y25 ~ b, data = sim), variables = "b")
ci_plot("y25", "9.l", show_p = TRUE)
```

:::

### Advice on confidence intervals and standard errors

- Most people---[including PhD researchers](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16392994)---do not understand what overlapping confidence intervals indicate about statistical significance
  - You need to recognize this when making graphics to present your findings
- *Importantly, when confidence intervals do not overlap (e.g., on the 1^st^ plot above) this indicates that the group difference (i.e., b~0~ vs b~1~) is significant*
  - *However, when the confidence interval does overlap this may or may not indicate the group difference is non-significant\*: you must test for this directly. As* [Belia et al. (2005)](http://psychology.okstate.edu/faculty/jgrice/psyc5314/ConfidenceConfusion_2005.pdf) *gently put it:*

![](images/belia-2005-abstract.png){width=80% fig-alt="Excerpt from the Belia et al. (2005) abstract: little is known about researchers' understanding of confidence intervals and standard error bars, and many leading researchers have severe misconceptions about how error bars relate to statistical significance."}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// 9.m - Add significance info to the graph using the text( ) option
*NOTE: specify the y-x coordinates for where to place text
coefplot, vertical ciop(recast(rcap) col(gs10)) ylab(45(1)60) ///
    xlab(1 "b = 0" 2 "b = 1") ytitle("y-hat") ///
    title("[9.m] Predictions and 95% Confidence Intervals - Linear Regression Model") ///
    text(53 1.5 "diff {it:p} = 0.032")
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/dmv-09_m-CIs_y25_text.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/dmv-09_m-CIs_y25_text.png){width=80% fig-alt="[9.m] The SD 25 predictions with the text diff p = 0.032 placed on the graph between the two groups."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[9.m] The SD 25 predictions with the p-value of the difference placed on the graph between the two groups."
# 9.m - Add the significance test of the difference to the graph itself
m25 <- lm(y25 ~ b, data = sim)
p25 <- avg_comparisons(m25, variables = "b")$p.value
ci_plot("y25", "9.m") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 53, label = paste0("diff p = ", round(p25, 3)))
```

:::
